mkdir -p /tmp/an && cat > /tmp/an/a.py <<'EOF'
import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'/srv/ml-training')
import torch, train
from torch import nn
torch.manual_seed(0)
f,m=train.make_data()
print("weekend ones", int((f[:,3]==1).sum()))
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16, 1))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
skipped=[];varied=0;last=None
for i,(b,t) in enumerate(train.batches(f,m)):
    w=b[:,3]
    if w.min()!=w.max(): varied+=1
    l=train.train_step(model,opt,b,t)
    if l is None: skipped.append((i,b.std(dim=0).tolist(),w.tolist()))
    else: last=(i,l)
print(skipped); print(varied,last)
EOF
.venv/bin/python -I /tmp/an/a.py

content.text:
I wrote `answers.json` with all eight answers and no nulls.

The run is fully reproducible because the data and the model both use fixed seeds. I replayed it from a script in `/tmp`, importing `train.py` without running its `main()`, so the existing `model.pt` was not overwritten. The replay's last loss was 379.23, which matches the "last loss 379.2" that was printed, so this is the same run.

| id | answer | why |
|---|---|---|
| q1 | 38 | 40 batches minus the 2 that were skipped |
| q2 | 2 | |
| q3 | [10, 11] | |
| q4 | weekend | That column's spread was 0 in both batches, so standardizing it divided 0 by 0 and turned the loss into NaN |
| q5 | 92 | rows with the weekend flag set to 1.0, out of 320 |
| q6 | 39 | the final batch, which wasn't skipped |
| q7 | 0.0 | every row in both skipped batches was a weekday |
| q8 | 38 | the other 38 batches all had both 0.0 and 1.0 |

The printed "trained 40 steps" overstates the training. The counter goes up even when a batch is skipped, so only 38 updates actually happened.
